issues.legal_issue: The restriction on a landlord’s successive applications for possession does not bar a later application where the tenant moved to another part of the same building under a settlement rather than vacating the building pursuant to an eviction order, or where a genuine new requirement has arisen.
material_facts: In an earlier eviction proceeding, the parties settled while the tenant’s appeal was pending; the tenant moved from the first floor to a room, kitchen, and passage on the ground floor of the same building.
The tenant’s move was not made under an eviction order, and the landlords did not obtain possession of the building through the settlement.
The landlords later sought possession for the first appellant’s family after its residential needs increased.
issues.conclusion: The third proviso did not bar the later eviction application; the tenant had not vacated the building and the landlords had not obtained possession under an eviction order. The restriction also does not prevent a later application based on a changed or new genuine requirement.
issues.legal_principle: The third proviso to Section 14(3) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987 applies where the landlord obtains possession of a building pursuant to an eviction order under the specified clauses; a tenant’s move to another part of the same building by settlement is not the tenant vacating the building or the landlord obtaining its possession. The proviso prevents a landlord from repeatedly relying on the same or similar circumstances after obtaining possession, but does not bar relief when the requirement has changed or a new, unrelated requirement has arisen. Molar Mal (dead) through L.Rs. v. M/s. Kay Iron Works (Pvt.) Ltd. was distinguished as not deciding this situation; the Court relied on the pragmatic approach to statutory interpretation in Rakesh Wadhawan v. Jagdamba Industrial Corporation and on the reasoning in Jagir Singh v. Jagdish Pal Sagar and Brij Lal Puri v. Smt. Muni Tandon.

rule.if: residential_own_occupation_eviction_case and (no_eviction_order_led_to_possession or tenant_did_not_leave_building or genuine_requirement_changed)

predicates.residential_own_occupation_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks possession of a residential premises for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.no_eviction_order_led_to_possession: The landlord did not obtain possession of the premises pursuant to an eviction order.
predicates.tenant_did_not_leave_building: The tenant moved to another part of the same building rather than leaving the building.
predicates.genuine_requirement_changed: The landlord’s genuine need materially changed or a new, unrelated genuine need arose.

issues.definition: When an own-occupation eviction proceeding involves a landlord who did not obtain possession through an eviction order, a tenant who did not leave the building, or a genuine changed requirement, the later application is not barred.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s occupation of another owned residential building bars an own-occupation eviction only when that accommodation is reasonably sufficient and suitable for the proven requirement.
material_facts: One appellant and his family occupied the upper floor, which had two rooms, a kitchen, and a verandah, and was already in use by that family.
The other appellant lived in rented accommodation with his family because of limited space and the inability of the two brothers’ families to live together.
The occupied accommodation was not reasonably capable of satisfying the residential needs of the appellant seeking possession for his family.
issues.conclusion: The first proviso did not bar eviction because the other accommodation was not reasonably sufficient and suitable to satisfy the proven requirement.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(3)(a)(i) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987 permits eviction where a residential building is required for the landlord’s own occupation, subject to the first proviso concerning another residential building owned and occupied by the landlord in the same urban area. The proviso must be read with the principal requirement ground: other accommodation defeats the claim only if it is reasonably enough and suitable to meet the proven need, not merely because it is occupied or technically available.

predicates.residential_own_occupation_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks possession of a residential premises for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.landlord_occupies_other_owned_residence: The landlord occupies another residential building that the landlord owns in the same urban area.
predicates.other_residence_unsuitable_for_proven_ne: The other residence is not reasonably sufficient and suitable for the landlord’s proven residential requirement.

issues.definition: If a landlord seeking residential premises for own occupation occupies another owned residence that is unsuitable for the proven need, that other accommodation does not disqualify the landlord.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord is not barred from seeking residential premises for own occupation by the restriction concerning a previously vacated building when vacation is not proved or occurred for sufficient cause.
material_facts: The tenant did not plead or prove that the landlords had vacated another residential building in the same urban area within the relevant period.
The ground-floor accommodation provided to the tenant under the settlement was not shown to have been a residential building actually occupied by the landlords.

The landlords agreed to the settlement while pursuing the earlier eviction proceeding and shifted the tenant to meet their then-existing need; the first appellant’s family later grew and its need changed.
issues.conclusion: The second proviso did not bar eviction: there was no sufficient pleading or evidence of a qualifying vacation, and the circumstances of the settlement amounted to sufficient cause in any event.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to Section 14(3)(a)(i) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987 concerns another residential building owned by the landlord in the same urban area, vacated without sufficient cause within the specified period. The tenant must plead and prove facts attracting the proviso; once that is done, the landlord may rebut the plea or prove sufficient cause. “Sufficient cause” is construed liberally to include a genuine and bona fide justifiable reason. The Court relied on Surinder Singh Sibia v. Vijay Kumar Sood for the meaning of “vacate” and “sufficient cause.”

predicates.residential_own_occupation_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks possession of a residential premises for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.qualifying_vacation_not_proved: The tenant has not established that the landlord vacated another owned residential building in the same urban area within the relevant period.
predicates.landlord_had_sufficient_cause_for_vacati: The landlord vacated the other building for a genuine and bona fide justifiable reason.

issues.definition: If a qualifying vacation is not established or the landlord had sufficient cause for it, the prior vacation does not disqualify the landlord from seeking possession.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s genuine residential requirement includes the need of the landlord’s family members.
material_facts: One appellant’s wife and children lived in rented accommodation because the other appellant’s family occupied the available upper-floor accommodation and the families could not suitably live together.
The first appellant’s family had grown, including the birth of another child, and the existing accommodation could not house that family.
The Rent Controller and Appellate Authority found the requirement bona fide, and the High Court did not dislodge those factual findings.
issues.conclusion: The residential need of the appellant’s family was the landlord’s own requirement, and the requirement for possession was made out.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “his own occupation” in Section 14(3)(a)(i) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987 is not confined to the landlord’s individual occupation; it includes the residential requirements of family members and dependants. The Court relied on Joginder Pal v. Naval Kishore Behal and Dwarkaprasad v. Nirnajan, which interpret comparable expressions to include the needs of the landlord’s family or dependants, and emphasized that the requirement must be genuine and bona fide.

predicates.residential_own_occupation_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks possession of a residential premises for the landlord’s own occupation.
predicates.landlord_genuinely_needs_home_for_family: The landlord genuinely requires the premises to house a family member or dependant.

issues.definition: When a landlord genuinely needs a home for a family member or dependant in an own-occupation eviction proceeding, that need counts as the landlord’s own occupation.
